html:
The tombs and mosques of the Qutb Shahi sultans of Golconda, in the Ibrahim Bagh garden just north of the outer wall of Golconda Fort, in Hyderabad. Seven of the eight sultans lie here. The first, Sultan Quli, built his own tomb in 1543, as was the custom, and set the pattern: a domed chamber on a square or octagonal base, ringed by pointed arches and raised on a terrace. The last sultan, Abul Hasan, died a prisoner of the Mughals at Daulatabad and was buried elsewhere; the tomb he began here holds another man.

The tombs blend Persian and Indian forms in carved stone, with galleries one or two storeys high. Their domes were once covered in blue and green tiles, of which only traces remain, and golden spires marked the sultans' tombs. The largest is that of Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, the builder of the Charminar, finished in 1602 on a terrace 4 m high. Also here are the tomb of the queen mother Hayat Bakshi Begum, a large mosque of 1666 with two tall minarets, and a mortuary bath where the bodies of the royal family were washed before burial.

In the reign of the dynasty the garden was a place of veneration, with carpets, chandeliers and Qur'an readers in the tombs. In 1687 the army of Aurangzeb besieging Golconda turned the tombs into barracks and mounted guns on them to fire at the fort, and the Mughal conquest ended the sultanate. Salar Jung III later had them repaired and walled. A long restoration by the Telangana archaeology department and the Aga Khan Trust for Culture began in 2013.
